name: Nintendo
note: Hanafuda card maker turned console giant whose internal R&D groups defined arcade, handheld and home-console design.

name: Nintendo R&D1
note: Gunpei Yokoi's group: Game & Watch, the Game Boy, Metroid and Wario; folded into SPD in 2003.

name: Nintendo R&D3
note: Hardware-leaning internal group behind Punch-Out!! and Super Mario RPG support work.

name: Nintendo R&D4
note: Miyamoto's original creative group, renamed Entertainment Analysis & Development in 1989.

name: Nintendo EAD
note: Miyamoto's flagship studio: Mario, Zelda, Wii Sports; merged into EPD in 2015.

name: Nintendo SPD
note: Software Planning & Development ran second-party partnerships and handheld titles until the 2015 EPD merger.

name: Nintendo EPD
note: Consolidation of EAD and SPD into one Entertainment Planning & Development division in 2015.

name: Sega
note: Arcade and console hardware maker that abandoned hardware in 2001 and became a third-party publisher.

name: Sony Computer Entertainment
note: Sony's games arm, created for the PlayStation; renamed Sony Interactive Entertainment in 2016.

name: Sony Interactive Entertainment
note: The PlayStation business after its 2016 reorganisation under a US-headquartered entity.

name: Microsoft
note: Software giant whose Xbox division became the industry's largest acquirer of studios.

name: Xbox Game Studios
note: Microsoft's first-party publishing label, renamed from Microsoft Game Studios to Microsoft Studios to Xbox Game Studios.

name: Activision
note: Founded by four Atari programmers denied credit and royalties; the first third-party console publisher.

name: Activision Blizzard
note: Created by Activision's merger with Vivendi Games and Blizzard; bought by Microsoft in 2023.

name: Electronic Arts
note: Trip Hawkins's 'software artists' label that became a serial acquirer of development studios.

name: Atari
note: Nolan Bushnell's company created the arcade and home-console markets before the 1983 crash.

name: Atari Games
note: The coin-op half of Atari after the 1984 split; ended as Midway Games West.

name: Take-Two Interactive
note: Publisher holding Rockstar Games and 2K; acquired Gearbox from Embracer in 2024.

name: ZeniMax Media
note: Holding company built around Bethesda Softworks; acquired by Microsoft in 2021.

name: Tencent
note: Chinese conglomerate owning Riot and Supercell outright plus minority stakes across the industry.

name: THQ Nordic
note: Nordic Games bought THQ's brands in 2013 and took the name; the parent later became Embracer.

name: Embracer Group
note: Acquisition machine that absorbed THQ, Deep Silver, Gearbox and Eidos before breaking itself apart.

name: Deep Silver
note: Koch Media's publishing label, home to Saints Row and Metro, bought by THQ Nordic's parent in 2018.

name: THQ
note: Toy Headquarters became a major publisher; its 2013 bankruptcy scattered studios to Nordic Games, Sega and Koch.

name: Kadokawa Corporation
note: Japanese media conglomerate; FromSoftware's majority owner since 2014.

name: Disney
note: Bought Lucasfilm in 2012 and shut LucasArts' development arm the following year.

name: Krafton
note: Bluehole renamed itself Krafton after PUBG's success and later bought Unknown Worlds.

name: Infogrames
note: French publisher that swallowed GT Interactive and Hasbro Interactive, then adopted the Atari name.

name: Vivendi Universal Games
note: Vivendi's games arm holding Blizzard and Sierra; merged into Activision Blizzard in 2008.

name: Konami
note: Jukebox repairer turned arcade and console publisher behind Metal Gear, Castlevania and Silent Hill.

name: Konami Computer Entertainment Japan
note: Konami's Tokyo development subsidiary during its late-1990s split into regional studios.

name: Capcom
note: Osaka arcade publisher whose Street Fighter and Resident Evil franchises defined two genres.

name: Namco
note: Arcade pioneer behind Pac-Man; merged its games business with Bandai's in 2006.

name: Bandai Namco Entertainment
note: The merged Namco and Bandai games business, renamed Bandai Namco Entertainment in 2015.

name: Square
note: Final Fantasy's creator, whose CD-ROM ambitions pushed it from Nintendo to Sony hardware.

name: Enix
note: Dragon Quest publisher that worked through contracted outside teams; merged with Square in 2003.

name: Square Enix
note: Product of the 2003 Square-Enix merger; bought Taito and Eidos, then sold its Western studios.

name: Taito
note: Space Invaders creator and arcade operator, acquired by Square Enix in 2005.

name: Koei Tecmo
note: Formed by the 2009 merger of strategy house Koei with Tecmo.

name: Tecmo
note: Ninja Gaiden and Dead or Alive publisher; merged into Koei Tecmo in 2009.

name: Midway
note: Brought Space Invaders to America and absorbed Williams and Atari Games before its 2009 bankruptcy.

name: Williams Electronics
note: Pinball and arcade maker behind Defender and Robotron; its video business merged into Midway.

name: Ubisoft
note: Guillemot brothers' distributor turned publisher running one of the largest global studio networks.

name: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
note: Warner's games label, owner of Rocksteady, Monolith and the DC and Middle-earth licences.

name: Softdisk
note: Louisiana disk-magazine publisher whose staff moonlighted on Commander Keen and then left to found id.

name: id Software
note: Carmack and Romero left Softdisk to build Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake; ZeniMax bought it in 2009.

name: Ion Storm
note: John Romero's post-id studio; its Austin office made Deus Ex before Eidos closed the company.

name: Raven Software
note: Wisconsin studio mentored by id Software on Heretic and Hexen; Activision's long-running Call of Duty support studio.

name: Apogee Software
note: Scott Miller's shareware publisher, which funded Commander Keen and Duke Nukem.

name: 3D Realms
note: Apogee's retail identity from 1996, remembered for Duke Nukem 3D and Duke Nukem Forever's fifteen-year development.

name: Gearbox Software
note: Founded by Randy Pitchford and other 3D Realms and Rebel Boat Rocker veterans; Borderlands' creator.

name: Gearbox Publishing
note: Gearbox's publishing arm, sold with the studio from Embracer to Take-Two in 2024.

name: Valve
note: Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington left Microsoft to make Half-Life; Steam later reshaped PC distribution.

name: Minh Le and Jess Cliffe
note: Counter-Strike's mod authors, hired by Valve when it bought the mod in 2000.

name: Eul, Steve Feak, IceFrog
note: Successive DotA modders; IceFrog joined Valve in 2009 to build Dota 2.

name: Facepunch Studios
note: Garry Newman's studio, born from the Garry's Mod sandbox built on Valve's Source engine.

name: Turtle Rock Studios
note: Left 4 Dead's creators; owned by Valve 2008-2010, then independent again, then bought by Tencent.

name: Bohemia Interactive
note: Arma's military-simulation developer, whose engine hosted the DayZ mod.

name: Dean Hall
note: Made the DayZ mod at Bohemia, turned it into a standalone hit, then left to found RocketWerkz.

name: PUBG Corporation
note: Studio built around Brendan Greene's battle-royale mods; absorbed into parent Krafton.

name: Sculptured Software
note: Utah licensed-games house, later Acclaim Studios Salt Lake City; three staff left in 1994 to found Neversoft.

name: Neversoft
note: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater studio, founded by ex-Sculptured staff; merged into Infinity Ward in 2014.

name: 2015, Inc.
note: Made Medal of Honor: Allied Assault for EA; most of the team then walked out to form Infinity Ward.

name: Infinity Ward
note: Founded by the 2015, Inc. Allied Assault team with Activision funding; created Call of Duty.

name: Respawn Entertainment
note: Founded by Infinity Ward's ousted heads Zampella and West; makers of Titanfall and Apex Legends.

name: Sledgehammer Games
note: Started by Visceral veterans Glen Schofield and Michael Condrey as a second Call of Duty studio.

name: Treyarch
note: Activision's third Call of Duty studio, creator of the Zombies mode and the Black Ops line.

name: Visceral Games
note: EA Redwood Shores renamed itself Visceral after Dead Space; EA closed it in 2017.

name: DMA Design
note: Dundee studio behind Lemmings and Grand Theft Auto; bought by Take-Two and renamed Rockstar North.

name: Rockstar Games
note: Take-Two's premium label, built by the Houser brothers around Grand Theft Auto.

name: Rockstar North
note: DMA Design under its Rockstar name, developer of Grand Theft Auto III onward.

name: Rockstar San Diego
note: Formerly Angel Studios; built the RAGE engine and Red Dead Redemption.

name: Rockstar Studios
note: Umbrella credit for Rockstar's globally merged development teams on recent releases.

name: BMG Interactive
note: Bertelsmann's short-lived games label; its GTA rights were sold to Take-Two.

name: Realtime Worlds
note: Founded by DMA's Dave Jones; made Crackdown before collapsing under APB.

name: Bungie
note: Halo's creators: independent, bought by Microsoft in 2000, independent again in 2007, then Sony in 2022.

name: 343 Industries
note: Formed by Microsoft to take custody of Halo after Bungie left.

name: Rare
note: Stamper brothers' studio, Nintendo's Western star of the 1990s, sold to Microsoft in 2002.

name: Mojang
note: Markus Persson's studio around Minecraft; sold to Microsoft for $2.5 billion in 2014.

name: Playground Games
note: Forza Horizon studio founded by racing-game veterans; acquired by Microsoft in 2018.

name: Ninja Theory
note: Heavenly Sword and Hellblade developer, bought by Microsoft in 2018.

name: Double Fine
note: Tim Schafer's studio after leaving LucasArts; joined Microsoft in 2019.

name: inXile Entertainment
note: Founded by Interplay's Brian Fargo; revived Wasteland before Microsoft acquired it.

name: Compulsion Games
note: Montreal studio behind Contrast and We Happy Few, acquired by Microsoft in 2018.

name: Good Science Studio
note: Microsoft's internal Kinect studio, creator of Kinect Adventures.

name: Ensemble Studios
note: Age of Empires developer; Microsoft bought it in 2001 and closed it in 2009.

name: Lionhead Studios
note: Peter Molyneux's post-Bullfrog studio; made Black & White and Fable before Microsoft closed it.

name: Bethesda Softworks
note: Publisher of The Elder Scrolls and Fallout; reorganised under holding company ZeniMax in 1999.

name: Bethesda Game Studios
note: Split out as Bethesda's in-house development arm; makers of Morrowind through Starfield.

name: Arkane Studios
note: Lyon studio that became the immersive sim's home after Looking Glass folded; makers of Dishonored.

name: MachineGames
note: Founded by Starbreeze veterans; rebooted Wolfenstein for ZeniMax.

name: Starbreeze Studios
note: Swedish studio behind The Chronicles of Riddick and Payday; lost its founding team to MachineGames.

name: Tango Gameworks
note: Shinji Mikami's studio, bought by ZeniMax then closed by Microsoft; revived under Krafton.

name: ZeniMax Online Studios
note: Built and still operates The Elder Scrolls Online.

name: Blue Sky Productions
note: Paul Neurath's studio; Ultima Underworld's first-person dungeon simulation started the immersive sim.

name: Looking Glass Technologies
note: Blue Sky merged with Lerner Research; made System Shock, Flight Unlimited and Thief's foundations.

name: Looking Glass Studios
note: Thief's creators, whose 2000 collapse scattered designers to Irrational, Ion Storm, Arkane and beyond.

name: Irrational Games
note: Ken Levine and two colleagues spun out of Looking Glass; made System Shock 2 and BioShock.

name: The Fullbright Company
note: Founded by the Irrational team behind BioShock 2's Minerva's Den; made Gone Home.

name: Interplay Entertainment
note: Brian Fargo's 'By Gamers. For Gamers.' publisher; home of Wasteland, Fallout and Baldur's Gate.

name: Black Isle Studios
note: Interplay's in-house RPG division: Fallout 2, Planescape: Torment and the Infinity Engine line.

name: Obsidian Entertainment
note: Founded by Black Isle leads after Interplay's decline; acquired by Microsoft in 2018.

name: Troika Games
note: Founded by Fallout's three creators after leaving Interplay; made Arcanum and Vampire: Bloodlines.

name: Blizzard Entertainment
note: Silicon & Synapse became Chaos Studios then Blizzard; Warcraft, StarCraft and World of Warcraft followed.

name: Blizzard North
note: Condor, renamed after Blizzard's parent bought it; created Diablo before its founders quit.

name: Flagship Studios
note: Founded by departing Blizzard North leads; Hellgate: London's failure sank it.

name: Runic Games
note: Built from Flagship's remains by Diablo veterans; made Torchlight under Perfect World's ownership.

name: Maxis
note: Will Wright's studio: SimCity, The Sims and Spore; absorbed by EA in 1997.

name: Bullfrog Productions
note: Molyneux's god-game studio (Populous, Dungeon Keeper), bought by EA and wound down by 2001.

name: Origin Systems
note: Richard Garriott's Ultima house; EA bought it in 1992 and closed it after Ultima Online.

name: Westwood Studios
note: Command & Conquer and Dune II creators; EA bought them in 1998 and shut them in 2003.

name: Petroglyph Games
note: Founded by Westwood staff after EA closed the studio; kept making real-time strategy games.

name: DICE
note: Digital Illusions grew from pinball games to Battlefield and the Frostbite engine.

name: Criterion Games
note: RenderWare engine maker turned Burnout and Need for Speed studio under EA.

name: BioWare
note: Founded by three medical doctors; Baldur's Gate, Mass Effect and Dragon Age followed before EA bought it.

name: Mythic Entertainment
note: Dark Age of Camelot's developer; EA bought it in 2006 and closed it in 2014.

name: EA Canada
note: Distinctive Software became EA's Vancouver sports factory behind FIFA and NHL.

name: EA Black Box
note: Black Box Games, bought by EA, made Need for Speed Underground and Skate.

name: DreamWorks Interactive
note: Spielberg's games venture created Medal of Honor; EA bought it and renamed it EA Los Angeles.

name: Codemasters
note: Darling brothers' budget publisher turned racing specialist; EA bought it in 2021.

name: 2D Boy
note: Two EA employees quit to make World of Goo, an early proof of indie viability.

name: Supergiant Games
note: Founded by EA Los Angeles veterans; Bastion, Transistor and Hades.

name: Naughty Dog
note: Jam Software became Naughty Dog: Crash Bandicoot, Jak, Uncharted and The Last of Us.

name: Insomniac Games
note: Spyro and Ratchet studio that stayed independent for 25 years before Sony bought it.

name: Polyphony Digital
note: Kazunori Yamauchi's Gran Turismo team, formalised as a Sony studio in 1998.

name: Media Molecule
note: Founded by Lionhead veterans; LittleBigPlanet and Dreams made players into creators.

name: Guerrilla Games
note: Killzone's developer, later the creator of Horizon Zero Dawn and the Decima engine.

name: Santa Monica Studio
note: Sony's internal studio behind God of War and an incubator for outside indie projects.

name: Sucker Punch Productions
note: Sly Cooper and inFAMOUS studio, acquired by Sony in 2011; later made Ghost of Tsushima.

name: Team Ico
note: Fumito Ueda's group inside Sony Japan Studio: Ico and Shadow of the Colossus.

name: Housemarque
note: Finland's oldest studio, arcade shooter specialists; Sony bought it after Returnal.

name: Psygnosis
note: Liverpool publisher of Lemmings and Wipeout; Sony bought it in 1993 to seed PlayStation development.

name: Sony Online Entertainment
note: EverQuest's operator; Sony sold it in 2015 and it became Daybreak.

name: Verant Interactive
note: Spun out of Sony's 989 Studios to run EverQuest, then folded back into Sony Online.

name: HAL Laboratory
note: Nintendo's close partner: Kirby and Smash Bros.; Satoru Iwata ran it before leading Nintendo.

name: Intelligent Systems
note: Nintendo-affiliated Kyoto studio behind Fire Emblem, Advance Wars and Paper Mario.

name: Game Freak
note: Fanzine turned studio; Pokemon made it Nintendo's most valuable independent partner.

name: Retro Studios
note: Texas studio set up with Nintendo funding; Metroid Prime saved it from closure.

name: Monolith Soft
note: Founded by Square's Xenogears team; Xenoblade's developer, majority-owned by Nintendo since 2007.

name: Sora Ltd.
note: Masahiro Sakurai's company, formed after leaving HAL, to keep directing Smash Bros.

name: Ape Inc.
note: Shigesato Itoi's Nintendo-backed studio behind EarthBound; became Creatures Inc.

name: Camelot Software Planning
note: Sonic! Software Planning left Sega for Nintendo, making Golden Sun and Mario sports games.

name: Chunsoft
note: Dragon Quest's original programmer-led developer; invented the sound novel and Mystery Dungeon.

name: Sonic Team
note: Sega's flagship internal studio, formed around Sonic the Hedgehog.

name: Sega AM2
note: Yu Suzuki's arcade group: Space Harrier, Virtua Fighter, Shenmue.

name: Sega AM3
note: Sega's arcade group behind Virtua Racing follow-ups and Crazy Taxi, later Hitmaker.

name: Smilebit
note: Formed from Team Andromeda and AM6; made Jet Set Radio and Panzer Dragoon Orta.

name: United Game Artists
note: Tetsuya Mizuguchi's Sega studio behind Rez and Space Channel 5; merged into Sonic Team.

name: Creative Assembly
note: Total War's developer, bought by Sega in 2005.

name: Atlus
note: Shin Megami Tensei and Persona house, acquired by Sega in 2013 after Index's collapse.

name: Rovio Entertainment
note: Angry Birds made mobile gaming mainstream; Sega bought the company in 2023.

name: Relic Entertainment
note: Homeworld and Company of Heroes studio, passed from THQ to Sega before a 2024 management buyout.

name: Ubisoft Montreal
note: Subsidy-backed studio that grew into Ubisoft's largest, home of Assassin's Creed and Far Cry.

name: Ubisoft Montpellier
note: Michel Ancel's studio: Rayman, Beyond Good & Evil.

name: Ubisoft Paris
note: Ubisoft's first internal studio; later made Just Dance and Ghost Recon Breakpoint.

name: Ubisoft Quebec
note: Quebec City studio that led Assassin's Creed Syndicate and Odyssey.

name: Red Storm Entertainment
note: Co-founded by novelist Tom Clancy; Ubisoft's 2000 purchase brought it the Clancy brands.

name: FreeStyleGames
note: DJ Hero and Guitar Hero Live developer, sold by Activision to Ubisoft and renamed Ubisoft Leamington.

name: Eidos Interactive
note: Tomb Raider's publisher, assembled from Domark and US Gold, bought by Square Enix in 2009.

name: Eidos-Montreal
note: Founded to continue Deus Ex and Thief; sold with Crystal Dynamics to Embracer in 2022.

name: Crystal Dynamics
note: Legacy of Kain and modern Tomb Raider studio, sold by Square Enix to Embracer in 2022.

name: Core Design
note: Derby studio that created Tomb Raider and lost it to Crystal Dynamics after Angel of Darkness.

name: U.S. Gold
note: Birmingham publisher importing American games to Europe; absorbed into Eidos.

name: IO Interactive
note: Hitman's developer; bought itself back from Square Enix in 2017 and kept the licence.

name: Sierra On-Line
note: Ken and Roberta Williams's adventure house; passed through CUC and Vivendi into Activision Blizzard.

name: Sierra Studios
note: Sierra's late-1990s label for action games including Half-Life and Homeworld.

name: Lucasfilm Games
note: George Lucas's games division; built SCUMM and the graphic-adventure style that rivalled Sierra.

name: LucasArts
note: Monkey Island and Star Wars games; Disney closed its development arm in 2013 after buying Lucasfilm.

name: Cyan
note: The Miller brothers made Myst, the CD-ROM era's defining bestseller.

name: Trilobyte
note: The 7th Guest's developer, an early full-motion-video CD-ROM success.

name: Delphine Software
note: French studio behind Another World's successor Flashback and cinematic platformers.

name: Infocom
note: MIT hackers who made text adventures literary; Activision bought and then dismantled them.

name: Broderbund
note: Publisher of Prince of Persia, Carmen Sandiego and Myst; sold to The Learning Company in 1998.

name: MECC
note: Minnesota's state education computing consortium, which made The Oregon Trail.

name: MicroProse
note: Sid Meier and Bill Stealey's simulation and strategy house: Civilization, Pirates!, X-COM.

name: Firaxis Games
note: Sid Meier, Jeff Briggs and Brian Reynolds left MicroProse; Civilization and XCOM continue there.

name: Strategic Simulations, Inc.
note: Wargame publisher that held the Dungeons & Dragons licence for the Gold Box RPGs.

name: New World Computing
note: Might and Magic and Heroes creators; died with its owner 3DO in 2003.

name: 3DO
note: Trip Hawkins left EA to license a console standard, then became a publisher until its 2003 bankruptcy.

name: Sir-Tech
note: Published Wizardry, the dungeon crawler that shaped Japanese RPG design.

name: Accolade
note: Founded by two of Activision's founders; won the landmark Sega reverse-engineering lawsuit.

name: GT Interactive
note: Retail publisher that made Doom a boxed hit; bought by Infogrames after overexpanding.

name: Gathering of Developers
note: Developer-run publisher formed as a protest against publisher control; absorbed by Take-Two.

name: Hasbro Interactive
note: Toy giant's games arm; bought Atari's and MicroProse's catalogues, then sold them to Infogrames.

name: Fox Interactive
note: News Corp's games label, publisher of The Simpsons Hit & Run and Aliens versus Predator.

name: MTV Games
note: Viacom's music-games label, formed around its purchase of Harmonix.

name: Harmonix
note: MIT spin-off that created Guitar Hero and Rock Band; bought by Epic in 2021.

name: RedOctane
note: Dance-pad maker that commissioned Guitar Hero; Activision bought it and dropped Harmonix.

name: Monolith Productions
note: No One Lives Forever, F.E.A.R. and Shadow of Mordor's Nemesis system; closed by Warner in 2025.

name: Rocksteady Studios
note: Batman: Arkham Asylum's developer, whose combat system became an industry template.

name: Volition
note: Descent's creators turned Saints Row studio; closed by Embracer in 2023.

name: Radical Entertainment
note: Vancouver studio behind The Simpsons: Hit & Run and Prototype, now an Activision support team.

name: Toys for Bob
note: Star Control's creators, later Skylanders and Crash; bought their independence back from Activision in 2024.

name: Bizarre Creations
note: Project Gotham Racing and Geometry Wars studio, closed by Activision in 2011.

name: Cavedog Entertainment
note: Total Annihilation's developer, a division of Humongous Entertainment under GT Interactive.

name: Simtex
note: Master of Orion and Master of Magic's developer, published by MicroProse.

name: Mythos Games
note: Julian Gollop's studio; X-COM's design came from his earlier Laser Squad work.

name: Cinematronics
note: Vector-graphics arcade maker that published Dragon's Lair's laserdisc animation.

name: Advanced Microcomputer Systems
note: Rick Dyer's company, which built Dragon's Lair around Don Bluth's animation.

name: Digital Pictures
note: Full-motion-video specialists whose Night Trap triggered the US Senate hearings on game violence.

name: Gottlieb
note: Pinball manufacturer whose arcade division produced Q*bert.

name: Muse Software
note: Baltimore publisher of Castle Wolfenstein, the stealth game id Software later revived.

name: subLOGIC
note: Bruce Artwick's company, whose Flight Simulator Microsoft licensed and eventually bought.

name: First Star Software
note: Publisher of Boulder Dash, an early cross-platform puzzle-action hit.

name: California Pacific Computer
note: Apple II publisher that released Richard Garriott's Akalabeth.

name: Quantum Link
note: Commodore 64 online service that hosted Habitat and later became America Online.

name: Acornsoft
note: Acorn's software arm, publisher of Elite on the BBC Micro.

name: Argonaut Games
note: Jez San's studio; its Super FX chip put polygons in Star Fox on the SNES.

name: Virgin Games
note: Richard Branson's games label, later renamed Virgin Interactive.

name: Virgin Interactive
note: Published Westwood's and Shiny's output before being carved up by Electronic Arts and Titus.

name: Team17
note: Amiga developer turned Worms custodian and prolific indie publisher.

name: Chris Sawyer Productions
note: Chris Sawyer wrote Transport Tycoon and RollerCoaster Tycoon almost entirely in assembly, alone.

name: FromSoftware
note: King's Field to Dark Souls and Elden Ring; Kadokawa owns it, with Sony and Tencent minority stakes.

name: SNK
note: Neo Geo hardware maker and fighting-game house behind King of Fighters and Metal Slug.

name: Irem
note: Arcade maker of R-Type and Kung-Fu Master, later a niche Japanese console publisher.

name: Technos Japan
note: Created the beat-em-up with Double Dragon and Kunio-kun.

name: Compile
note: Puyo Puyo and Aleste developer, bankrupted in 2003 with its puzzle brand sold to Sega.

name: Natsume
note: Developer and publisher associated with Harvest Moon's Western releases.

name: Nippon Ichi Software
note: Disgaea's creator, a specialist in deep strategy RPGs for a small dedicated audience.

name: Team Ninja
note: Tecmo's action studio: Ninja Gaiden, Dead or Alive and Nioh.

name: Team Silent
note: The internal Konami group that made the first four Silent Hill games, then dissolved.

name: Kojima Productions
note: Hideo Kojima's studio inside Konami, refounded as an independent company after their 2015 split.

name: Clover Studio
note: Capcom's auteur studio: Viewtiful Joe and Okami; closed after commercial disappointment.

name: PlatinumGames
note: Founded by Clover's departing staff; Bayonetta, Nier: Automata and Metal Gear Rising.

name: Level-5
note: Professor Layton and Ni no Kuni developer that became its own publisher.

name: Cavia
note: Drakengard and Nier developer whose staff carried Yoko Taro's work into Square Enix projects.

name: Climax Entertainment
note: Landstalker and Dark Savior developer, an early isometric action-RPG specialist.

name: NanaOn-Sha
note: Masaya Matsuura's studio, which invented the rhythm game with PaRappa the Rapper.

name: Light Weight
note: Small Japanese studio best known for Bushido Blade's realistic sword duelling.

name: Amccus
note: Small Japanese developer of console strategy and simulation titles.

name: HoYoverse
note: Shanghai students' anime-styled studio; Genshin Impact made free-to-play gacha a global business.

name: NetEase Games
note: Chinese internet giant's games arm, both a huge domestic publisher and a global studio investor.

name: Youthcat Studio
note: Chinese developer of the narrative puzzle game Nobody - The Turnaround.

name: Gamera Game
note: Chinese indie publisher that brought domestic titles like Dyson Sphere Program abroad.

name: NCSoft
note: Lineage's developer, the company that made subscription MMOs a mass market in Korea.

name: Nexon
note: Pioneered free-to-play with microtransactions through MapleStory and Dungeon Fighter.

name: Neowiz
note: Korean publisher whose Round8 studio made Lies of P.

name: Round8 Studio
note: Neowiz's internal studio, developer of Lies of P.

name: Wizet
note: MapleStory's developer, absorbed into Nexon.

name: Mintrocket
note: Nexon's experimental studio, which made Dave the Diver.

name: CD Projekt
note: Started as a Polish game importer, then built GOG and became a global publisher.

name: CD Projekt Red
note: The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077 studio, formed to adapt Sapkowski's novels.

name: 11 bit studios
note: This War of Mine and Frostpunk developer, focused on morally uncomfortable survival design.

name: Bloober Team
note: Polish horror specialist behind Layers of Fear and the Silent Hill 2 remake.

name: Superhot Team
note: Turned a game-jam prototype about time moving only when you move into Superhot.

name: Larian Studios
note: Divinity developer that spent two decades reaching Baldur's Gate 3.

name: Paradox Interactive
note: Grand-strategy publisher built on long-tail expansion sales for its own and others' games.

name: Paradox Development Studio
note: Paradox's in-house team: Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, Hearts of Iron, Stellaris.

name: Avalanche Studios
note: Just Cause's developer, specialists in large open worlds and physics-driven destruction.

name: Coffee Stain Studios
note: Goat Simulator and Satisfactory developer, acquired by THQ Nordic's group in 2018.

name: Coffee Stain Publishing
note: Coffee Stain's publishing arm for Deep Rock Galactic, Valheim and other indie hits.

name: Raw Fury
note: Stockholm indie publisher known for author-friendly terms and stylised games.

name: Iron Gate Studio
note: Five-person team whose Valheim sold millions within weeks of early access.

name: Arrowhead Game Studios
note: Magicka and Helldivers developer, built on friendly fire as a design principle.

name: Embark Studios
note: Founded by ex-EA and DICE head Patrick Soderlund; Nexon funded and then bought it.

name: Frictional Games
note: Penumbra, Amnesia and Soma; made powerlessness the core of modern horror games.

name: Playdead
note: Limbo and Inside's creators, wordless monochrome puzzle-platformers.

name: Geometric Interactive
note: Founded by Limbo and Inside's lead designer Jeppe Carlsen; made Cocoon.

name: Ghost Ship Games
note: Deep Rock Galactic's developer, a co-op-first Copenhagen studio.

name: Remedy Entertainment
note: Demoscene group turned studio: Max Payne, Alan Wake and Control.

name: Colossal Order
note: Independent Tampere studio, published by Paradox, that took the city-builder crown with Cities: Skylines.

name: Supercell
note: Small-cell mobile studio behind Clash of Clans; Tencent bought a majority stake in 2016.

name: Nolla Games
note: Three Finnish developers built Noita's every-pixel-simulated falling-sand world.

name: Hempuli
note: Arvi Teikari, whose Baba Is You turns the game's own rules into pushable blocks.

name: CCP Games
note: EVE Online's operator, running a single shared universe with a player-driven economy.

name: Crytek
note: The Yerli brothers' studio; Far Cry and Crysis defined PC graphical benchmarks.

name: Piranha Bytes
note: Gothic and Risen's developer, closed during Embracer's restructuring.

name: BeamNG GmbH
note: Soft-body vehicle physics specialists whose crash simulation became a research tool.

name: Motion Twin
note: French worker cooperative behind Dead Cells, with equal pay and no hierarchy.

name: Asobo Studio
note: Bordeaux studio behind A Plague Tale and Microsoft Flight Simulator's 2020 revival.

name: Focus Entertainment
note: French mid-tier publisher of A Plague Tale, Vermintide and other AA titles.

name: Eric Chahi
note: Made Another World alone, inventing cinematic rotoscoped storytelling on the Amiga.

name: Rundisc
note: Small French team behind the linguistics puzzle game Chants of Sennaar.

name: MercurySteam
note: Madrid studio entrusted with Castlevania: Lords of Shadow and Metroid Dread.

name: The Game Kitchen
note: Seville studio whose Blasphemous fuses Andalusian religious imagery with Metroidvania design.

name: GSC Game World
note: Kyiv studio behind S.T.A.L.K.E.R., which built its open zone from Chernobyl's real geography.

name: 4A Games
note: Founded by GSC programmers; the Metro series carried the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. lineage abroad.

name: Battlestate Games
note: Escape from Tarkov's developer, pushing extraction shooters toward simulation.

name: Owlcat Games
note: Pathfinder and Rogue Trader CRPG developer, staffed by Russian industry veterans.

name: META Publishing
note: Indie publisher backing eastern European projects including Pathologic and Loop Hero.

name: Wargaming
note: World of Tanks maker; free-to-play vehicle combat built a huge eastern European audience.

name: ZA/UM
note: Writers and artists collective whose Disco Elysium replaced combat with skills that argue.

name: Wube Software
note: Factorio's developer, whose factory-automation loop spawned an entire genre.

name: Beat Games
note: Beat Saber's two-person developer, acquired by Facebook's Oculus division in 2019.

name: Jagex
note: RuneScape's developer; browser-based Java MMO play reached players without gaming PCs.

name: Introversion Software
note: Bedroom-coder revivalists behind Uplink, Darwinia and Prison Architect.

name: Hello Games
note: No Man's Sky's small team, which spent years turning a disastrous launch around.

name: Chucklefish
note: Starbound's developer and the publisher that first brought Stardew Valley to market.

name: Mediatonic
note: Fall Guys' developer, bought by Epic in 2021.

name: The Chinese Room
note: Dear Esther and Everybody's Gone to the Rapture; the studio the 'walking simulator' label followed.

name: ustwo games
note: Design agency's games arm, whose Monument Valley proved premium mobile art games could sell.

name: Playstack
note: London publisher that signed and released Balatro.

name: Kinetic Games
note: Phasmophobia's developer, whose voice-recognition ghost hunting became a streaming phenomenon.

name: poncle
note: Luca Galante's label; Vampire Survivors turned an idle bullet-heaven loop into a genre.

name: Galactic Cafe
note: Released The Stanley Parable, a game about narration and the illusion of player choice.

name: Shedworks
note: Two-person London studio behind the desert exploration game Sable.

name: Bigmode
note: Publisher founded by YouTube critic videogamedunkey to fund small distinctive games.

name: Egmont Interactive
note: Danish media group's short-lived games publishing arm.

name: Strategy First
note: Montreal strategy publisher, best known for Disciples and Space Empires.

name: Behaviour Interactive
note: Montreal's largest independent studio; Dead by Daylight made asymmetric horror a live service.

name: Digital Extremes
note: Unreal's co-developer, later self-funding Warframe; Tencent acquired its parent Leyou.

name: Klei Entertainment
note: Don't Starve and Oxygen Not Included studio; sold a majority stake to Tencent in 2021.

name: United Front Games
note: Vancouver studio that finished Sleeping Dogs after Activision cancelled it.

name: Typhoon Studios
note: Journey to the Savage Planet's developer, bought by Google Stadia and closed a year later.

name: Red Barrels
note: Outlast's developer, which stripped combat out of first-person horror.

name: Studio MDHR
note: The Moldenhauer brothers remortgaged a house to hand-animate Cuphead in 1930s cartoon style.

name: Cellar Door Games
note: Rogue Legacy's developer, which popularised persistent progression in roguelites.

name: Brace Yourself Games
note: Crypt of the NecroDancer's developer, binding dungeon movement to the music's beat.

name: Kitfox Games
note: Montreal studio and publisher, custodian of Dwarf Fortress's commercial release.

name: Trapdoor
note: Montreal studio behind Warp and Fable Fortune.

name: Ludeon Studios
note: Tynan Sylvester's studio; RimWorld's AI storyteller generates colony drama procedurally.

name: LocalThunk
note: Anonymous solo developer of Balatro, a poker roguelike built as a hobby project.

name: Andrew Shouldice
note: Solo developer of Tunic, an isometric adventure whose manual is its central puzzle.

name: Polytron Corporation
note: Phil Fish's studio; Fez and Indie Game: The Movie defined the 2012 indie moment.

name: Team Bondi
note: L.A. Noire's developer, whose facial-capture ambition and crunch culture ended the studio.

name: Team Cherry
note: Three Adelaide developers made Hollow Knight after a game jam, funded by Kickstarter.

name: House House
note: Melbourne collective behind Untitled Goose Game.

name: Alexander Bruce
note: Solo creator of Antichamber, a first-person puzzle game built on impossible geometry.

name: ConcernedApe
note: Eric Barone spent four years alone building Stardew Valley, then self-published it.

name: Toby Fox
note: Undertale's solo creator, who wrote its music, code and morality system himself.

name: 3909 LLC
note: Lucas Pope left Naughty Dog to make Papers, Please and Return of the Obra Dinn.

name: Team Meat
note: Edmund McMillen and Tommy Refenes made Super Meat Boy, indie's breakout console success.

name: Edmund McMillen
note: Designer of Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Isaac, which set the roguelite template.

name: Nicalis
note: Publisher that brought Cave Story and The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth to consoles.

name: Number None
note: Jonathan Blow's company for Braid, the game that opened the Xbox Live Arcade indie wave.

name: Thekla, Inc.
note: Jonathan Blow's studio for The Witness, an island of nothing but line puzzles.

name: Mossmouth
note: Derek Yu's label; Spelunky brought procedural generation to the platformer.

name: Subset Games
note: Two ex-2K China developers made FTL on Kickstarter, then Into the Breach.

name: 2K Games
note: Take-Two's second label, holding BioShock, Civilization, Borderlands and the NBA 2K series.

name: Devolver Digital
note: Austin publisher of provocative indies, known for satirical E3 press conferences.

name: Annapurna Interactive
note: Film financier's games label backing authored, emotionally driven titles.

name: Finji
note: Rebekah and Adam Saltsman's family studio and publisher: Canabalt, Night in the Woods, Tunic.

name: Hooded Horse
note: Publisher specialising in strategy and simulation games including Manor Lords.

name: Panic
note: Mac software company that published Firewatch and Untitled Goose Game, then built the Playdate.

name: Adult Swim Games
note: The cable network's games label, publisher of Rain World, Duck Game and Headlander.

name: Campo Santo
note: Firewatch's developer, founded by Telltale and Klei veterans and absorbed by Valve.

name: Giant Sparrow
note: Made The Unfinished Swan and What Remains of Edith Finch under Sony's incubation.

name: thatgamecompany
note: Formed by USC students with a Sony contract; Flower and Journey pushed games toward emotion.

name: InnerSloth
note: Three-person studio whose Among Us became a hit two years after release.

name: Re-Logic
note: Terraria's developer, which kept shipping free content updates for over a decade.

name: Unknown Worlds Entertainment
note: Natural Selection modders turned studio; Subnautica made underwater survival mainstream.

name: Mobius Digital
note: Outer Wilds' developer, built around a 22-minute solar-system time loop.

name: Hopoo Games
note: Risk of Rain's developer, whose escalating-difficulty design shaped co-op roguelites.

name: Mega Crit Games
note: Slay the Spire's developer, which fused deckbuilding with roguelike runs.

name: Sirvo
note: Asher Vollmer's team behind Threes, the sliding-number puzzle 2048 cloned.

name: Imangi Studios
note: Husband-and-wife studio whose Temple Run defined the endless runner.

name: Bay 12 Games
note: The Adams brothers' Dwarf Fortress simulates history, geology and dwarven madness in ASCII.

name: Freehold Games
note: Caves of Qud's developer, a science-fantasy roguelike with deep procedural lore.

name: Shining Rock Software
note: Luke Hodorowicz built the city-builder Banished alone over three years.

name: Parsec Productions
note: Mark Hadley's Slender: The Eight Pages seeded a decade of internet-folklore horror games.

name: Videocult
note: Rain World's developer, built around a hand-animated ecosystem indifferent to the player.

name: Dogubomb
note: Solo studio behind Blue Prince, a shifting-mansion roguelike puzzle game.

name: Billy Basso
note: Spent seven years alone building Animal Well's dense interlocking secret world.

name: Zeekerss
note: Solo developer of Lethal Company, whose proximity voice chat drove its viral spread.

name: Squad
note: Mexican advertising firm's side project became Kerbal Space Program; Take-Two later bought it.

name: Terry Cavanagh
note: Made VVVVVV and Super Hexagon, minimalist games built on one punishing mechanic.

name: Mike Bithell
note: Made Thomas Was Alone in his spare time, proving rectangles could carry characterisation.

name: Moon Studios
note: Distributed studio behind Ori and the Blind Forest and No Rest for the Wicked.

name: Slavic Magic
note: Greg Styczen built Manor Lords, a medieval city-builder, almost entirely alone.

name: Pocketpair
note: Craftopia and Palworld's developer, whose creature-collecting survival hybrid drew Nintendo's lawsuit.

name: Dennaton Games
note: Two-person team behind Hotline Miami's neon top-down violence.

name: Extremely OK Games
note: Maddy Thorson's studio, which grew Celeste from a four-day game jam prototype.

name: dotGEARS
note: Dong Nguyen's label; Flappy Bird's viral success led him to pull it from stores.

name: Eleventh Hour Games
note: Last Epoch's developer, an action RPG built by fans of the Diablo lineage.

name: Hi-Rez Studios
note: Smite and Tribes: Ascend developer, an early free-to-play shooter and MOBA operator.

name: Psyonix
note: Rocket League's developer, bought by Epic in 2019.

name: Epic Games
note: Potomac Computer Systems became Epic MegaGames then Epic Games; Unreal, Fortnite and a 40% Tencent stake.

name: Epic Games Publishing
note: Epic's publishing label offering full funding and even revenue splits to outside studios.

name: Riot Games
note: Built League of Legends from the DotA mod; Tencent took majority control in 2011 and all of it in 2015.

name: King
note: Candy Crush Saga's maker, bought by Activision Blizzard for $5.9 billion in 2016.

name: Roblox Corporation
note: User-generated game platform whose creators build and monetise experiences for a young audience.

name: Niantic
note: Spun out of Google in 2015; Ingress's map data became Pokemon Go.

name: Yacht Club Games
note: WayForward veterans Kickstarted Shovel Knight, a model for revivalist 8-bit design.

name: Gunfire Games
note: Founded by Vigil Games staff after THQ's collapse; Darksiders III and Remnant.

name: Cryptic Studios
note: City of Heroes' developer, later a Perfect World and Embracer MMO studio.

name: 505 Games
note: Italian publisher that brought Terraria, Payday and Death Stranding's PC release to market.

name: Alexey Pajitnov
note: Wrote Tetris at a Soviet research centre and saw no royalties for a decade.

name: Academy of Sciences of the USSR
note: Its Moscow Computing Centre employed Alexey Pajitnov and owned Tetris's early rights.

name: David Braben and Ian Bell
note: Cambridge students whose Elite fitted a procedural galaxy of trade and combat into 22 kilobytes.

name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman, Ken Arnold
note: Berkeley students whose Rogue gave its name to procedurally generated permadeath dungeons.

name: Steve Russell / MIT
note: MIT hackers wrote Spacewar! on a PDP-1 in 1962, the first widely copied digital game.

name: Jordan Mechner
note: Rotoscoped his brother to animate Prince of Persia after Karateka's success.

name: Richard Garriott
note: Created Ultima as 'Lord British' and founded Origin Systems to publish it.

name: Douglas E. Smith
note: Wrote Lode Runner as a student, adding a level editor that made players designers.

name: Blue Byte
note: The Settlers and Anno developer, bought by Ubisoft in 2001 and now Ubisoft's German arm.

name: Pandemic Studios
note: Star Wars Battlefront and Mercenaries studio, bought with BioWare by EA and closed in 2009.

name: Free Radical Design
note: Founded by Rare's GoldenEye programmers; made TimeSplitters before collapsing and being revived twice.

name: Ready at Dawn
note: Founded by Naughty Dog and Blizzard veterans; God of War handheld games, The Order: 1886, then VR.

name: Bluepoint Games
note: Remake and remaster specialists (Shadow of the Colossus, Demon's Souls), acquired by Sony in 2021.

name: Nixxes Software
note: PC porting house for Eidos and Square Enix titles, bought by Sony in 2021.

name: Bend Studio
note: Eidetic became Sony Bend: Syphon Filter, Uncharted: Golden Abyss and Days Gone.

name: Team Fortress Software
note: Robin Walker and John Cook's Quake mod team, hired by Valve to build Team Fortress Classic.

name: tinyBuild
note: Indie publisher behind Hello Neighbor and Punch Club, built on streamer-driven marketing.

name: Zachtronics
note: Zach Barth's studio, which made programming and engineering puzzles into a genre.
